source.title: More findings on maximal data dimension

record.file_problem: The prose is readable, but the figures referenced in the post are not present in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The author explicitly says they replicate the double-descent experiment, using the ReLU Output model and a dataset-size sweep, with stated changes to the original setup.
record.gate_note: The post explicitly reports reproducing double descent in its adapted setting. It does not give numerical test-error values or a detailed description of the plotted curve in the supplied text. Results about D* itself, including its shape across dataset sizes, are not test-error results and are not recorded as rows. Findings cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The post reruns a dataset-size sweep in the Anthropic toy ReLU Output model with 1000 features and sparsity 0.99. It reports that double descent reappears. This is a toy superposition setting, not the original sources' method, so it is a new-setting replication of sample-wise double descent (T3), not T1. Its evidence is only a textual statement because the figures and numbers are missing.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but the post's focus is the D* metric, not double descent. The double-descent reproduction is context. The author concludes that D* likely captures something meaningful. Two findings remain unexplained: misclassified training points spread evenly or left-heavy across D*, and D* changes little from initialization through training. These need follow-up.
record.recipe_differences: The post adapts the ReLU Output-model setup: it uses 1000 rather than 10000 features, sparsity 0.99 rather than 0.999, and cuts off the dataset-size range earlier.
record.method_sensitivity: The post states that the schedulers described in the referenced paper make a difference, but does not specify their effect on the reported double-descent result.

fits_no_version.finding: The double-descent peak shifts 10x earlier in dataset size when the feature count is cut 10x (10000 to 1000).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy superposition models, the dataset size at which the double-descent peak occurs scales with the number of features.

fits_no_version.finding: D* (maximal data dimensionality) separates memorized datapoints from generalizing ones across the double-descent dataset-size sweep. Before the transition the curves are high and flat; after it they are lower and sloped.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A per-datapoint dimensionality metric tracks the switch from memorization to generalization at the double-descent transition.

record.problems: The figures are absent from the supplied text, and the post gives no numerical test-error results or uncertainty estimates for the double-descent reproduction. It also modifies the original experiment's feature count, sparsity, and dataset-size range.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version rows were omitted. D* findings and training-iteration misclassification findings were left out because they do not report test-error behavior named by the claim.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep of test error. Hidden-size sweeps on MNIST report only D*, loss and accuracy shapes, not a double-descent curve.
No test error over training time.
Magnitude of the rise in test error, the location of the interpolation threshold, and any real-data setting.
No effective-complexity measure is tested across axes.
No label noise, no multiple peaks, and no optimally tuned regularization. Weight decay is studied only for its effect on D*.

record.verdict_notes: This is an Alignment Forum blog post, and the figures are absent from the supplied text. The double-descent evidence is a single sentence with no numbers. The main study object is a replication of the Anthropic toy-model setup (transformer-circuits 2023), not of the listed original sources. Most of the post concerns D* on MNIST and does not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep of test error is reported.
Training-iteration results concern D* and misclassification distributions, not test error over epochs.
The post does not give numerical test-error values or specify the interpolation-threshold location.
No comparison of double descent across model classes is reported.
The post does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
Weight decay is examined for its effect on D*, not on the double-descent peak; label noise, multiple peaks, and optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
No re-counting of complexity or test of whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve is reported.

rows.subject: ReLU Output model
rows.operation_detail: Varied dataset size in an adapted double-descent experiment.
rows.measure: Double-descent phenomenon; specific error measure not stated
rows.value: The double descent happens exactly 10x earlier than in the original paper.
rows.note: The author attributes the shift to using 10x fewer features. The post says the phenomenon was reproduced but does not provide test-error values in the supplied text.
rows.check: Subject and conditions are correct. The measure is unstated; the referenced Anthropic setup plots test loss against dataset size, but the post gives no values or baseline. The quoted value describes the peak's location (10x earlier), not its size, so the state rests only on the author's statement that double descent was reproduced.

relationships.reason: r1: the author states the data-wise double descent was reproduced. The basis is text only, with no numbers or figures available.
relationships.display_finding: The author reports reproducing double descent as dataset size varies.
